extracted.intended_audience: education institutions and Title IX administrators (K-12 and postsecondary), school legal counsel, Title IX coordinators
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and requirements for recipient grievance procedures under Title IX, including timeframes, extensions, privacy protections, evidence access, supportive measures, and related training and notice obligations for K-12 and postsecondary institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonably prompt timeframes for major stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must set, and abide by, reasonably prompt timeframes for the major stages of their grievance procedures; timeframes must be reasonable and for good cause, and recipients may only provide reasonable extensions for good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeframes are important for setting expectations and facilitating participation; procedures must not be indefinite. Prompt resolution furthers Title IX's nondiscrimination mandate. Recipients retain flexibility to establish specific reasonably prompt timeframes; some may use 60 days but recipients may set shorter or longer periods based on context. Supportive measures are available during the pendency of grievance procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensions for good cause and notice requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may grant reasonable extensions of timeframes on a case-by-case basis for good cause; recipients must notify parties of the reason for the extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 106.46(e)(5) requires postsecondary recipients subject to the Clery Act to provide written notice of a reasonable extension of timeframes for good cause that includes the reason for the delay. The final rules allow extensions for good cause but do not permit indefinite procedures or hiding reasons for extension. The Department removed enumerated examples of good cause to avoid implying mandatory extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: No statute of limitations on filing a sex discrimination complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to adopt a statute of limitations for filing sex discrimination complaints under Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying a statute of limitations could be unfair to complainants who may wait to pursue a grievance for a variety of reasons; the final regulations safeguard fairness and reliability without imposing a filing time limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of major stages of the grievance procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients should identify major stages of their grievance procedures—evaluation, investigation, determination, and appeal—and may identify additional stages if helpful to set expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department slightly revised wording for clarity: the evaluation stage is described as 'the recipient's decision whether to dismiss or investigate a complaint of sex discrimination' to avoid multiple uses of 'determination.' Recipients may provide timeframes for additional stages if it aids transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial evaluation as a major stage with a timeframe
rubrics_metrics.description: The recipient's initial evaluation of whether to dismiss or investigate a complaint constitutes a major stage and parties should be aware of the timeframe governing when that evaluation will be completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For promptness and transparency, recipients should include the evaluation stage timeframe in grievance procedures so parties understand when that decision will occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: No mandatory delay for concurrent law enforcement proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are not required to delay Title IX grievance procedures because of an ongoing law enforcement proceeding; they also are not prohibited from delaying for good cause on a case-by-case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A concurrent law enforcement proceeding may sometimes justify good-cause extensions, but not always. Recipients are encouraged to avoid extensions when possible. Regardless, recipients must continue to offer and provide supportive measures and may need to take actions to ensure access to education during law enforcement proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures must not be delayed by law enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must not delay the provision of supportive measures because of a concurrent law enforcement proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures (see §106.44(f)(1)(ii), (g)) should continue as appropriate to restore or preserve a party's access to education or to provide support during grievance procedures or informal resolution, even if an extension is granted for investigation timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on adverse inference from silence
rubrics_metrics.description: A decisionmaker is prohibited from drawing an inference about whether sex-based harassment occurred based solely on a party's or witness's refusal to respond to questions deemed relevant and not impermissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See §106.46(f)(4) for the prohibition and related discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: No regulatory definition of 'prompt', 'good cause', or 'reasonable' timeframes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to define 'prompt,' 'good cause,' or 'reasonable' in the regulations, leaving recipients flexibility to determine appropriate timeframes in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meaning depends on specific contexts; recipients should determine what is prompt or reasonable in light of providing an education program free from sex discrimination. The Department removed specific examples of good cause to avoid implying they are mandatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of circumstances that may justify extensions (good cause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good cause for an extension may include, for example, reasonable extensions to accommodate the absence of a party, a party's advisor, or a witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating extensions, recipients should consider ways to avoid extensions (e.g., allowing videoconference participation or requiring an advisor with sufficient availability). Recipients should provide reasonable modifications for disabilities and language assistance within established timeframes when possible without extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to file OCR complaint for failure to comply with timeframes
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone who believes a recipient failed to comply with reasonably prompt timeframes set forth in its grievance procedures may file a complaint with the Office for Civil Rights (OCR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides enforcement for the requirement that recipients set and follow reasonably prompt timeframes and only allow reasonable extensions for good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable steps to protect privacy during the pendency of grievance procedures (§106.45(b)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are required to take reasonable steps to protect the privacy of the parties and witnesses during the pendency of grievance procedures, provided such steps do not restrict parties' ability to obtain and present evidence, consult with family/confidential resources/advisors, or otherwise prepare for or participate in the grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is reasonable depends on the circumstances; recipients must assess whether a given step is reasonable and whether it impermissibly restricts evidence-gathering, consultations, or participation. Any steps infringing constitutional rights or undermining due process are inherently unreasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy-protection steps may not restrict parties' rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(5) prohibits a recipient from taking steps to protect privacy that restrict the parties' ability to gather evidence, consult with certain individuals, or prepare for or participate in the grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although §106.45(b)(5) does not apply to steps taken for purposes other than privacy protection, other provisions protect such rights—e.g., §106.45(f)(2) (opportunity to present witnesses/evidence), §106.46(e)(2) (advisor accompaniment), and §106.6(g) (parents/guardians/legal reps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of 'confidential resource' vs 'confidential employee'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Confidential resource' is not synonymous with 'confidential employee'; a confidential resource need not be an employee but must have confidential status under Federal, State, local law, or by virtue of their profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers or friends generally will not qualify as confidential resources; mental health counselors or community-based rape crisis counselors generally will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'advisor' for privacy and participation purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Advisors' refers to any individual acting as an advisor to the party for purposes of the grievance procedures, including but not limited to the advisor of the party's choice referenced in §106.46.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should interpret 'advisor' broadly for the purposes of consultation and preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wording clarified to 'otherwise prepare for or participate in the grievance procedures'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department replaced 'prepare for a hearing, if one is offered' and 'otherwise defend their interests' with 'otherwise prepare for or participate in the grievance procedures' to avoid overbroad interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change narrows misuse of 'defend their interests' as a justification for widespread disclosures and clarifies parties' consultation rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap and interaction of privacy-related provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must comply with overlapping requirements in §§106.45(b)(5), 106.45(f)(4)(iii), and 106.46(e)(6)(iii), which set privacy protections and obligations to prevent/address unauthorized disclosures of material obtained solely through grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some steps to protect privacy may satisfy multiple provisions; recipients should ensure steps to prevent unauthorized disclosures are reasonable and consistent across provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redaction and disclosure rules for evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may redact information that is not relevant to the allegations but must not redact evidence that is relevant to the allegations and not otherwise impermissible; certain categories must be redacted or not used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must redact or refrain from disclosing privileged information, records made by physicians/psychologists in connection with treatment, or evidence about complainant's sexual interests or prior sexual conduct (with narrow exceptions). Due process and parties' rights to access relevant evidence may in some cases justify disclosure even if inconsistent with FERPA (constitutional and GEPA overrides).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment records use limited to voluntary written consent
rubrics_metrics.description: A party's or witness's records made or maintained by a physician, psychologist, or other recognized professional or paraprofessional related to treatment must not be accessed, considered, disclosed, or otherwise used as part of the grievance procedures unless the party/witness provides voluntary, written consent for use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See §106.45(b)(7)(ii) and related discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nondisclosure agreements: neither required nor prohibited but limited
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations neither require nor prohibit nondisclosure/confidentiality agreements; recipients may use them at their discretion but must comply with all regulatory requirements and cannot condition supportive measures or initiation of grievance procedures on signing such agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overly broad NDAs may not satisfy §106.45(b)(5)'s reasonableness requirement. If a recipient requires an NDA, it must still comply with disclosure, privacy, and other procedural requirements of the regulations and applicable laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy protections temporal scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(5)'s requirement to take reasonable steps to protect privacy applies during the pendency of grievance procedures but does not extend beyond their conclusion; other provisions (e.g., §106.44(j)) and other privacy laws continue to apply after conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After conclusion, disclosure presents less threat to fairness and integrity of investigation; Title IX still prohibits harassment and retaliation post-conclusion. FERPA and other laws may limit disclosures unless Constitutional/GEPA overrides apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training on grievance procedures and privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must ensure employees and individuals who have any role in implementing the Title IX regulations receive training on the recipient's grievance procedures (§106.8(d)(2)(ii)), which includes privacy-related training obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Department declined to prescribe detailed privacy-training content, the regulations require training related to responsibilities under the grievance procedures; recipients may provide additional training on other privacy laws or methods to protect sensitive data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient notice obligations about grievance procedures and privacy steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must inform parties of the grievance procedures and reasonable steps to protect privacy as part of the notice requirements (e.g., §§106.44(f)(1)(iii) and 106.45(c)(1)(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear notices help parties understand procedures, timeframes, and privacy protections; written notice of extensions is specifically required in §106.46(e)(5) for postsecondary recipients subject to the Clery Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on disciplinary or administrative actions that infringe due process or constitutional rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Any steps taken to protect privacy or otherwise implement procedures that infringe constitutional rights or otherwise undermine due process are inherently unreasonable and not permitted under the regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must avoid privacy steps that would restrict constitutional rights or due process protections; such steps do not qualify as 'reasonable steps' under §106.45(b)(5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Retaliation and deliberate delays
rubrics_metrics.description: An intentional delay in grievance procedures could constitute retaliation if it meets the definition of 'retaliation' in §106.2 (e.g., imposed for a retaliatory motive), but the Department declined to enumerate additional specific types of retaliation in §106.71.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of whether a delay is retaliatory require fact-specific analysis against the general retaliation standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient authority to take actions during pendency to ensure access
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must operate education programs free from discrimination and may need to take actions during the pendency of grievance procedures (including emergency removal of a respondent under §106.44(h)) to ensure students' access to education is not limited or denied based on sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such actions must be consistent with the regulations' requirements, including supportive measures and due process protections.
